cards.title: Use dynamic call tracking for phone-assisted ecommerce purchases
cards.summary: Dynamic phone-number replacement attributes purchase-assistance calls to the session, channel, campaign, and—in some setups—paid keyword that generated them.
cards.use_when: Measuring a store where shoppers call to ask product, sizing, delivery, financing, or high-ticket purchase questions before ordering.
steps: Install a dynamic call-tracking tool such as ResponseTap on the store, verifying its current implementation requirements and pricing first. The tool replaces the displayed phone number for each visitor session with a temporary number using the same area code.

Configure reporting to associate a call with the shopper's entry page, the page on which they called, and acquisition source. Where supported, connect Google Ads data to identify campaign and keyword context.
Integrate call events with your analytics and advertising measurement so calls are visible as assisted conversion events rather than disappearing as untracked offline activity.

Record calls only in accordance with applicable consent and privacy rules. Review recordings to identify product-page questions, recurring objections, sales-team gaps, and whether particular channels generate purchase-ready callers.
If the full tool is not economical, use click-to-call tracking or a platform forwarding number as a lower-cost but less complete alternative.
caveats: The source cited roughly £250 per month for ResponseTap at the time; assess whether call volume and paid-media spend justify it.
A phone call is not automatically a purchase. Where possible, connect calls to subsequent orders rather than treating every call as equal revenue.

cards.title: Add live chat with deliberate coverage hours
cards.summary: Live chat can remove pre-purchase friction when it is staffed during defined hours, routed to available people, and treated as a measurable support-to-purchase path.
cards.use_when: Adding real-time help to PDPs, cart, or checkout for shoppers with questions about fit, stock, shipping, compatibility, returns, or product choice.
steps: Choose a chat tool such as Tawk.to and verify its current free-tier terms, routing features, and installation method before deploying the site code.
Set explicit online hours based on when a trained team member can answer. Outside those hours, use a message option rather than implying immediate support is available.
Create separate team accounts and use round-robin routing or another ownership rule so chats reach an available person rather than remaining unanswered.
Equip agents with current answers for product specifications, shipping cutoffs, returns, and common objections. Route questions that require order lookup or specialist advice appropriately.
Use the mobile app only if it supports reliable response quality; convenience should not result in slow or incomplete answers.
Track chat starts, topics, escalation rate, and downstream orders where your tools allow. Use repeated questions to improve PDP content, shipping copy, and FAQs.
caveats: Chat is useful only when somebody can respond competently during the hours shown.
The source describes Tawk.to as free because it also sells staffed chat services; pricing and product terms may change.

cards.title: Audit ecommerce pages with the CLOSER checklist
cards.summary: Use credibility, lure, objection handling, social proof, ease of use, and result as a qualitative framework for finding purchase friction on PDPs, category pages, cart, and landing pages.
cards.use_when: Prioritizing CRO work on a product page, paid landing page, cart, or checkout before deciding what to test.
steps: Review credibility: establish why the store or product should be trusted through relevant expertise, secure-payment cues, clear policies, recognizable retailers or press, and truthful product claims.
Review the lure: identify what makes the immediate action attractive, such as a product benefit, bundle, delivery offer, first-order incentive, or buyer guide for visitors not ready to buy.
Review objection handling: address likely fears around fit, compatibility, quality, dispatch speed, returns, warranty, pricing, or how the product is used.
Review social proof: make it clear that other relevant shoppers have bought and valued the product, using reviews, customer photos, usage volume, or credible endorsements.
Review ease of use: inspect variant selection, stock clarity, add-to-cart visibility, form burden, shipping-cost visibility, and checkout impediments.

Review result: state what happens after the action—what the buyer receives, when it dispatches, how it is delivered, and what the product outcome is. List gaps, then turn the most consequential uncertainties into test hypotheses.
caveats: CLOSER is a source-provided qualitative checklist, not a weighted score or proof that a change will lift conversion.
Use analytics, session evidence, and controlled testing to validate changes rather than treating checklist completion as optimization.

cards.title: Treat every product and category landing page as a cold-traffic destination
cards.summary: Do not rely on the homepage to establish trust or explain the offer, because search, shopping ads, social ads, and shared links often send shoppers directly to an inner page.
cards.use_when: Optimizing PDPs, collection pages, product-led paid landing pages, or SEO pages that can receive visitors who have never seen the store before.
steps: Use analytics to identify product and category pages with direct, organic, paid, or referral entrances; prioritize pages with meaningful traffic or commercial intent.
On each priority page, make the product, audience, and primary benefit immediately clear without requiring visitors to infer context from navigation or brand familiarity.

Place relevant trust assets on the page itself: authentic reviews, return and shipping information, secure-payment reassurance, relevant press or retailer proof, and product-specific customer examples where available.
Add a clear, product-specific action and make the outcome understandable: selected variant, price, delivery expectation, return protection, and the next step after add-to-cart.
Use service-specific proof analogously for products: proof should relate to that product or category rather than being generic homepage decoration.
Evaluate the page with the CLOSER checklist and test the largest gaps, particularly missing credibility, unclear outcomes, or a weak path to purchase.
caveats: The source demonstrated the issue with a service subpage; this is an ecommerce application of the same direct-landing principle, not a reported ecommerce result.
Choose proof that is genuine and relevant; logos or generic claims cannot substitute for product information.

cards.title: Design store navigation as product guidance, not a directory
cards.summary: Navigation should use shopper language and guide people toward the right product or category instead of presenting a long, internally organized list of choices.
cards.use_when: Restructuring a store menu with many collections, technical product types, or category names that shoppers may not recognize.
steps: Audit menu length and identify points where shoppers face too many competing choices. The source argues that long option lists cause people to forget earlier options and make wrong selections.
Replace internal terminology, supplier terminology, and jargon with words shoppers use when describing the need, use case, product type, or recipient.
Do not default to alphabetical ordering when it conflicts with discovery. Put popular, seasonal, high-margin, or decision-critical categories where shoppers can find them easily.
Send a menu click to the most useful destination: usually the relevant collection, curated category, or buying-guide page—not a vague intermediary page that forces another navigation decision.
For shoppers who do not know the correct product name, add need-state routes such as use case, problem, compatibility, size, or gift recipient, where appropriate.
Validate changes with navigation-path data, site search terms, session recordings, and category conversion rather than assuming a shorter menu is always better.
caveats: The source's examples concern service navigation, so category structures and labels must be adapted to the store's assortment and shopper vocabulary.
A menu change can affect SEO, merchandising, and returning-customer habits; monitor those effects.

cards.title: Research paid-ad landing pages for testable ecommerce patterns
cards.summary: Competitor paid ads can reveal pages designed for commercial conversion, providing hypotheses about messaging, proof, offers, and purchase flow without proving those tactics will work for your store.
cards.use_when: Planning a PDP or landing-page redesign, entering a category, or seeking concrete CRO hypotheses for paid-traffic destinations.
steps: Search commercially relevant category and product keywords, then inspect paid ads and their destination pages. Advertisers are paying for traffic, making these pages useful candidates for studying conversion intent.
Document each page's promise, hero message, product explanation, offer, review presentation, shipping and returns treatment, CTA placement, and checkout or add-to-cart path.
Evaluate the pages with CLOSER: credibility, lure, objection handling, social proof, ease of use, and result. Record specific patterns rather than copying visual style.
Pay particular attention to what occurs after the primary action: cart behavior, delivery clarity, bundle prompts, email capture, and reassurance before checkout.
Use observations to formulate narrowly scoped hypotheses for your own store—for example, whether clearer application instructions reduce hesitation on a technical PDP.
Benchmark against your own current page and test changes with appropriate sample size and commercial metrics such as purchase conversion, revenue per visitor, and margin impact.
caveats: A paid ad does not prove that its landing page is profitable or well measured.
The source notes that a visually unattractive page with an exceptionally easy form may outperform more polished pages; prioritize shopper clarity and friction over design imitation.

cards.title: Sell familiar ecommerce products by explaining, proving, and de-risking them
cards.summary: A product with established demand still needs a PDP that clearly explains use and benefit, shows credible proof, addresses practical objections, and makes the ownership outcome tangible.
cards.use_when: Building or improving a PDP for a commodity-like, technical, novel-in-use, or easily compared product.
steps: Explain how the product works in plain language, supported by concise benefit-led copy, icons, and application or setup instructions. The source's Shark Proof example used explanation of how its wipe-on screen protector was applied.

Show credible proof close to the buying decision: authentic customer reviews, secure checkout signals, substantiated bestseller or units-sold claims, and product-specific demonstrations where available.

Handle operational objections explicitly with real policies and capabilities, such as return window, dispatch timing, shipping availability, warranty, and support. Do not imply benefits your operation cannot deliver.
Make use friction visible and solvable. If shoppers may wonder whether a product is easy to apply, install, clean, or maintain, provide clear steps and, where appropriate, demonstration media.
Make the intended result concrete. For protective or performance products, show evidence of the product performing under the conditions buyers care about.
Check currency, price, and shipping-origin cues for contradictions that could create uncertainty about where the order ships from or what it will cost.
caveats: The source raised a credibility concern where reviews appeared concentrated around similar dates; review volume alone is not reliable proof.
The Shark Proof observations are illustrative, not evidence that these elements produced a measured uplift.

cards.title: Capture not-ready shoppers with a consideration-matched email offer
cards.summary: Use email capture to retain shoppers who are not ready to purchase, matching the incentive to whether they need help choosing or simply need a reason to buy later.
cards.use_when: Designing PDP, collection-page, or exit-intent email capture for products with a meaningful consideration cycle or future replenishment and launch potential.
steps: Separate visitors who do not know what to buy from those who know the product but are postponing purchase. Their signup incentives should solve different problems.
For uncertain shoppers, offer a useful buyer guide or decision aid in exchange for email. Make it genuinely relevant to choosing among products, variants, sizes, or technical specifications.

For shoppers who know what they want but are delaying, test an economically viable first-order benefit such as a percentage discount or free postage. Calculate expected margin impact before deploying it broadly.
Use signup data and browsing context to send relevant future messages: product education, restocks, launches, seasonal reminders, and appropriate replenishment prompts.
The source suggested that a technology-focused store could offer useful tips, Apple rumors, or new-product release alerts; adapt this idea to content your customers would plausibly value.
Measure signup rate as a supporting metric, then evaluate incremental purchase conversion, revenue, discount cost, and margin—not just list growth.
caveats: The source gives no conversion evidence for buyer guides, discounts, or free shipping, and does not establish whether offers should be combined or mutually exclusive.
For inexpensive impulse products, an additional email step may be unnecessary or distract from immediate purchase.

input.source_name: COMPLETE Revenue-increasing Conversion Rate Optimisation (CRO) Course.docx

cards.title: Assess whether a high sales close rate reflects a narrow lead funnel
cards.summary: A very high sales conversion rate means you attract only pre-qualified leads; widen the lure and expect more unqualified leads.
cards.use_when: Reviewing a sales-assisted or lead-generation journey; this is not a rule for ecommerce checkout conversion.
steps: Treat the presenter's high-close-rate claim as a hypothesis: compare qualified lead volume, sales capacity and acquisition economics before broadening the funnel.

Check your sales conversion rate. If it is near 100% or very high, treat it as a red flag: your marketing funnel is not wide enough and you are only attracting people who have already qualified themselves.
Widen the top of the funnel or make the lure more attractive so more people enter earlier in their awareness journey.
Expect the number of unqualified leads to increase. This is normal and comes with a larger number of qualified leads; don't treat it alone as a failure.
If you are not getting objections such as 'you're not right for me', your funnel is still too narrow. Expand it until you attract people who are not yet sure.
caveats: A wider funnel requires a plan for unqualified leads; otherwise you may frustrate your sales team.
This is the source's heuristic, not a universal numeric rule.
A high close rate alone does not prove the funnel is too narrow. Do not broaden acquisition solely to lower this percentage.

cards.title: Build a Plan B to monetize unqualified and not-ready leads
cards.summary: Monetize leads you cannot serve directly through training, lower-tier offers, referral commissions, and long-term email nurture.
cards.use_when: Your wider funnel produces leads that are unqualified, low-budget, outside your area, or not ready now.
steps: Segment the unqualified leads: budget mismatch, geography, need you don't serve, or timing.

Create an alternative monetization route. Example: Exposure Ninja created Marketing You, a training site, so people who could not afford done-for-you marketing could learn to do it themselves and later potentially become clients.
Refer leads you cannot serve to competitors or partners for an affiliate or referral commission. Exposure Ninja receives referrals from other agencies and pays commission on leads it sends out.

Build a long-term email sequence (the source calls it an indoctrination sequence) that runs over days, weeks, months, or years to move people toward seeing you as the best logical choice. Exposure Ninja has had clients on its list for five to six years before buying.
caveats: Requires ongoing content and email effort.
Not every lead will convert later; this is a monetization layer, not a guarantee.

cards.title: Use a four-step sales process after lead capture for service businesses
cards.summary: Map the post-lead sale as assessment, check-in, proposal, and check-in/close to turn website leads into clients.
cards.use_when: Designing what happens after a prospect fills a form for a service business.
steps: Assessment: understand the scale of the problem and help the prospect identify what their solution might look like.
Check-in: get feedback on the assessment, answer questions, check whether it met expectations, and start identifying objections that may come later.
Proposal: make a plan or suggestion for working together. The source notes 'pitch' is a poor word; frame it as a plan.
Check-in after the proposal: ask what they thought and use this call to close the sale.
Exposure Ninja's process follows this: marketing review, phone call to debrief, marketing plan, then a call after the plan.
caveats: This structure is for service companies; e-commerce businesses adapt it differently.
Customize each step to your sales cycle and team capacity.

cards.title: Compress the four-step sales process when the prospect already knows what they need
cards.summary: Combine assessment and check-in into one call to make a three-step process if the prospect already understands their problem.
cards.use_when: Your prospects already know what they need and do not require a separate assessment step.
steps: Decide whether the prospect already knows the scale of their problem or exactly what they need. If yes, combine the assessment and check-in into the initial phone call.

Exhibition stand company example: initial phone call covers assessment and check-in; then they produce a stand design mockup and price as the proposal; then a follow-up call or email checks in and asks to proceed.
Holiday business example: fact-finding call covers assessment and check-in; proposal contains the price and holiday plan; final check-in happens by phone or email depending on ticket size.

High-volume automated example: PPI claims company processed about 400 leads per day. Assessment was an information pack sent to the lead; check-in and proposal were covered by a notification of PPI claim amount plus an order form. No human interaction; all automated by letters and emails.
caveats: Match the level of human touch to volume and ticket size; high-touch does not scale at very high lead volume.
The source presents these as examples, not one-size-fits-all rules.

cards.title: Map your sales process before optimizing the website's first step
cards.summary: Know how you will turn leads into sales before creating a high-converting site, or you will create leads you cannot convert.
cards.use_when: You are about to build or optimize a lead-generating website and need to align it with your sales process.
steps: Write out your sales steps using the assessment / check-in / proposal / check-in-close structure as a prompt.
Answer: How do you cover your assessment? What form does the next check-in take? How do you present your proposal? What form does the post-proposal check-in take, and where will you close?

Ensure the website's first step (the lure) delivers what your sales process needs. Do not just create a high-converting website if you do not know how to turn those leads into sales; that creates stress and frustration.
For e-commerce businesses, run the same process but sign people up for your email list, newsletter, or contact details instead of making them a lead.
caveats: The source focuses on service companies but explicitly adapts the idea to e-commerce email signup.
The adaptation to e-commerce is not detailed step-by-step in the source.

cards.title: Use ResponseTap for dynamic call tracking and attribution
cards.summary: ResponseTap swaps phone numbers per visitor session to attribute phone calls to page, source, keyword, and campaign.
cards.use_when: Phone calls are a primary conversion action and you need to know which marketing produced them.
steps: Install ResponseTap code on your website. When a visitor lands, the code switches out your displayed phone number for a temporary virtual number using the same area code.

If that visitor calls the virtual number, ResponseTap can associate the call with that specific session. It reports the entry page, the page they converted on when they called, traffic source, and for Google Ads the keyword and campaign.
Integrate with Google Analytics so a phone call appears as a conversion, and therefore in Google Ads. Record calls to quality-check your sales team and assess lead quality by marketing channel.
If budget is limited, use click-to-call tracking or a Google forwarding number. These are free but less scientific than ResponseTap.
caveats: ResponseTap costs around £250 per month in the source's example. Only worth it if you generate enough call leads and need attribution, especially if spending on PPC.
Verify current pricing and interface, as tool details may change.

cards.title: Use a callback widget to capture and increase phone calls
cards.summary: A Live Call-style widget lets visitors request an immediate callback and can also increase direct phone calls.
cards.use_when: You have a sales team ready to take calls and want an additional low-friction conversion path.
steps: Install a call widget such as Live Call. Set triggers, for example after a visitor has been on the site for a certain time or scrolls down the page.
Visitor enters their phone number and clicks 'call me now'. The system calls your team first and whispers caller information, then dials the visitor and connects both parties.
Calls can be recorded if needed. The source observed that simply offering to call people back also increased the number of people who called the main phone number directly.
Test it on your site. It is cheap relative to many tools; the source cites $49 per month on the annual plan at the time.
caveats: Only works if you have people on the phones and ready to take calls during set hours.
Verify current pricing and availability.

cards.title: Use Tawk.to for free live chat with scheduled hours
cards.summary: Tawk.to is a free live chat tool with round-robin routing, scheduled availability, and a mobile app.
cards.use_when: You want live chat but do not want to be tied to your computer at all hours or pay for software.
steps: Sign up for Tawk.to and add the code to your site. The source describes it as free and as powerful as many paid tools.
Set your opening and closing hours. Chat is only online during those hours; outside them, visitors can leave a message.
Create team accounts so multiple people can receive chats. Tawk.to can round-robin incoming chats among available agents.
Use the mobile app to answer chats from your phone.
caveats: Tawk.to makes money by selling live chat staffing, so the free software model may change. Verify current terms and interface.
You still need someone available during scheduled hours for live chat to work.

cards.title: Use Leadpages alert bars and landing pages for sitewide CTAs
cards.summary: Leadpages alert bars and landing pages let non-technical marketers add sticky sitewide CTAs and standalone paid-traffic pages.
cards.use_when: You need a sitewide call to action or landing pages but cannot easily add forms or build pages in your website platform.
steps: Design an alert bar or landing page in Leadpages. For an alert bar, add the provided code to your site header.
The alert bar sticks to the top or bottom of the page on desktop and mobile, making a sitewide call to action visible at all times.
Use it for lead capture, such as a free consultation, email signup, or click-to-call options. You can combine credibility elements like review widgets in the same bar.
Build standalone landing pages in Leadpages for paid traffic with a large, focused call to action.
Test the alert bar against forms built directly into the page.
caveats: The source says an alert bar may not convert as well as a form built into the page, but it should convert better than no call to action.
Verify current Leadpages interface and code placement.

cards.title: Audit pages with the six-element CLOSER checklist
cards.summary: Evaluate any page on credibility, lure, objection handling, social proof, ease of use, and result.
cards.use_when: Doing a CRO teardown, prioritizing page improvements, or comparing your page with competitors.
steps: Credibility: How many credibility triggers are present? Is it clear the business has reason to talk about the topic?
Lure: How attractive is the thing used to get the visitor to become a lead?
Objection handling: Are potential fears or objections about requesting the offer removed?
Social proof: Is it obvious that other people have chosen this business?
Ease of use: How easy is it to become a lead or sale? Are there impediments?
Result: Is it clear what result the visitor will get when they take the desired action?
Work through each element for a page, note gaps, and prioritize fixes based on the weakest elements.
caveats: This is a qualitative framework from the source, not a weighted scoring system.
Use it as a prompt, not as a substitute for testing.

cards.title: Treat service subpages as landing pages ready for cold traffic
cards.summary: Assume inner service pages receive direct or organic traffic and must carry credibility, social proof, lure, and a clear CTA on their own.
cards.use_when: Optimizing service pages that rank in search or receive paid traffic.
steps: Identify pages that can receive cold traffic directly, such as commercial contracts or other service subpages.
Add credibility assets to those pages: awards, Trustpilot reviews, client logos, and names. Do not rely on the homepage to carry these.
Include a clear lure and call to action on each service page, with service-specific case studies showing logos and work done for that particular service.
Example: Owen Mitchell's homepage had awards and Trustpilot credibility, but the commercial contracts page lost all of that when reached directly. It also had no lure or trackable CTA.
Do not assume visitors navigate from the homepage through your menu. Many will land directly on the subpage.
caveats: The source uses one solicitor example; adapt which credibility assets matter to your sector.
Case-study logos can give credibility even if visitors do not read the full case study.

cards.title: Design menus to guide, not to act as a directory
cards.summary: Avoid long alphabetical menus; too many options confuse visitors and lead to wrong clicks.
cards.use_when: Structuring site navigation, especially service menus with many categories.
steps: Limit menu options. The source compares too many options to a phone menu with more than six choices: people forget what earlier options were.
Do not alphabetize categories unless there is a natural reason. Put popular items where they can be found, not where the alphabet puts them.
Use plain language that visitors understand, not internal or legal jargon.
Send category clicks to the actual category page, not to a 'commercial home' page. Terms like that are web-development language, not customer language.
Help visitors who do not know what their issue is called to find the right information. A menu should guide; a directory just lists pages.
caveats: Navigation should match users' mental models; test changes.
The source example is a solicitor site, but the principle applies broadly.

cards.title: Replace email-link CTAs with tracked forms and booking
cards.summary: Email-link CTAs block tracking and can prevent conversions; use forms and booking tools instead.
cards.use_when: Your main call to action opens an email client or is simply an email address.
steps: Replace mailto links with a contact form that captures name, email, optional phone, and a message.

Position the form near the page content. The source suggests a scrolling contact form in the whitespace at the side of the page, with wording such as: 'If you need help with commercial contracts, fill in your details here and one of the commercial contracts team will be in touch to arrange a free consultation at no charge or obligation at a convenient time for you.'
Make the phone field optional and use a simple send button.
Consider a booking tool such as Calendly so visitors can lock in a time with your business development team. The source says this improves show-up rate.
Track form submissions as conversions; email-client clicks cannot be reliably tracked and may fail if the visitor's email platform is not configured.
caveats: Email links may still be appropriate in some contexts, but they usually reduce tracking and ease of conversion.

cards.title: Write page headings with full context, not internal shorthand
cards.summary: Page titles and headings must state the service and audience; assume the visitor has no context.
cards.use_when: Writing or reviewing headings for service pages and homepages.
steps: Avoid vague headings such as 'Commercial contracts' or 'Expert hand, human touch'. These do not tell a cold visitor what the business does.
Write descriptive headings such as 'Commercial contract solicitors' so the visitor immediately knows the service and who it is for.
Check that the heading makes sense to someone who landed directly from Google with no knowledge of your brand or menu structure.
Ensure the homepage also states what the business does without requiring the visitor to hunt through the menu.
Review menu labels and page titles for internal jargon that customers would not understand.
caveats: The source gives a solicitor example; the same principle applies to other service pages.

cards.title: Study paid ads to find conversion-focused landing pages
cards.summary: Clicking competitors' paid ads reveals pages that must convert, giving useful CRO patterns and examples.
cards.use_when: Researching a niche, looking for landing page inspiration, or benchmarking against competitors.
steps: Search a target keyword and click the paid ads at the top of the results. Advertisers are paying for traffic, so they are more likely to be tracking and optimizing.
Analyze each ad landing page using the six-element checklist: credibility, lure, objection handling, social proof, ease of use, and result.
Note what the page promises, what happens after form submission, and how easy it is to act.

Example: a lead-generation firm in the legal niche had Trustpilot credibility, a simple form, 24/7 availability, and stated it had helped 17,000 businesses. Its page outperformed a solicitor website that had spent far more on design.
Also note that an ugly page with a very easy form can outperform others if it nails ease of use, even if other elements are weak.
caveats: Advertisers are examples, not guarantees; some may not track well.
Use the patterns as hypotheses to test on your own site.

cards.title: Sell a commoditized ecommerce product like a new concept
cards.summary: Even products with established demand need strong selling; Shark Proof shows how to explain, prove, and handle objections on a product page.
cards.use_when: Building or optimizing an ecommerce product page, especially for a product buyers think they already understand.
steps: Explain how the product works and its benefits, using icons and clear descriptions. Shark Proof explains how its screen protector is wiped onto a phone.
Add credibility: customer reviews, safe checkout logos, best-seller status, and units sold. Shark Proof shows 'over 500k sold'.
Handle objections directly: 30-day easy returns, same-day dispatch, and free worldwide shipping.
Provide clear application instructions to reduce the fear of 'how easy is this to use?'
Make the result clear. Shark Proof could have gone further by showing video of people attacking phones with knives while the protector is on.
Consider offering email signup for people not ready to buy now, such as technology tips or alerts for new phone releases.
Check that currency and price cues do not create a shipping-origin objection. Shark Proof priced in pounds but showed a $75 figure, making a UK buyer wonder if it ships from the US.
caveats: The source notes Shark Proof's reviews all appeared around similar dates, which raised a credibility concern.
These are examples, not measured guarantees.

cards.title: Offer an ecommerce email signup for visitors not ready to buy
cards.summary: Use the lead-generation process but sign people up for email with a buyer guide, discount, or free shipping.
cards.use_when: Ecommerce visitors are not ready to purchase now but could buy later.
steps: Identify the not-ready-now segment. They may not know what to buy, or they know but are not ready to purchase yet.
If they do not know what to buy, offer a free buyer guide download in exchange for email.
If they know what they want, offer a 10% first-order discount or free first-order postage in exchange for email signup.
Build the list for future product launches or seasonal campaigns. Example: Shark Proof could create a technology tips blog or offer free Apple rumors and new product release alerts.
For cheap impulse products, this may not be necessary, but the option is available if your product has a longer consideration cycle.
caveats: The source gives no conversion data for buyer guides, discounts, or free postage.
Whether discount and free postage are combined or mutually exclusive is not stated; test.

cards.title: Lead gen CTA must state what the visitor gets and what happens next
cards.summary: A lead capture page should state the result and the post-submission process, not just 'we'll call you'.
cards.use_when: Creating or auditing a lead generation landing page.
steps: State what the visitor will get. Examples from the source include a free claim assessment, a free consultation, or a price.
State what happens after they submit: who will contact them, how, and when. The source criticizes a page that said 'we'll call you' but did not say when or what the result would be.
Add credibility and social proof near the CTA. The source notes Trustpilot, review volume, and statements like 'we've helped 17,000 businesses'.
Make the form easy to use and above the fold, with 24/7 availability if possible.

Example: a lead generation firm had a simple form, Trustpilot, 24/7 availability, and 17,000 businesses helped, but fell down on result clarity because it did not say what the visitor would get or when they would be called.
Even a page that only nails ease of use can outperform a page with no optimization, but combining elements is stronger.
caveats: The source uses examples, not measured promises.
Do not overpromise; clarity about the next step is the goal.
